scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

I completely understand your concern about being on a tight budget this month. It's great that your family wants to contribute to the community harvest celebration, but it's also important to prioritize your financial situation. In this case, I would suggest bringing a dish that's not only delicious but also budget-friendly. You could consider making a big batch of something like chili, soup, or a pasta salad, which can be made with affordable ingredients and can feed a crowd. Another idea is to get creative with what you already have at home. Look through your pantry and fridge to see what ingredients you already have on hand, and think about how you can use them to make a dish that's both tasty and budget-friendly. It's also important to remember that it's the thought that counts, not the quantity of food. Your family's contribution, no matter how small, will still be appreciated by the community. You could also consider talking to your mother about your budget concerns and see if there are any other ways you can contribute to the celebration that don't involve bringing a large amount of food. Ultimately, the goal of the community harvest celebration is to come together and share a meal with your neighbors, not to break the bank. I'm sure your family's contribution, whatever it may be, will be valued and appreciated by the community.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
